newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian industry demands sugar price deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Indian industry demands sugar price deregulation.

text.p: The Indian sugar industry urged the government on Tuesday to deregulate sugar prices to reduce fluctuations in output and make exports competitive.
Vivek Saraogi, president of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), said the government had recently ended a company's monopoly over sugar export trade and might delicense production.
"But there is no discussion whatsoever on sugar (price) decontrol," he told an international sugar conference.
Production and pricing of sugar in India are controlled by the government.

The mills supply 40 percent of their output as levy at a subsidised rate for distribution among the poor. The government controls the release of the remainder on the free market through the use of sales quotas.
Under an economic liberalisation programme which was launched in 1991, India began abolishing licences for many industries. But it kept sugar under the old regime.

Last month the government decided to "decanalise" exports by ending the monopoly over foreign sales belonging to the Indian Sugar and General Industries Export Import Corp (ISIGEC), a private company set up by the sugar milling industry.
In the future, any firms registered with the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) will be able to export sugar.
"Decanalisation of exports without decontrol (of prices) makes little sense," Saraogi told the Asia International Sugar Conference in New Delhi.
Saraogi said Indian sugar could become competitive in the international market only when sugar prices were decontrolled.
"In the regime of decontrol, Indian sugar will be more competitive in the international market," said S.L. Jain, another senior ISMA official.
Jain said price decontrol would reduce fluctuations in sugar output, stabilise supplies and make India a regular exporter.
India is expected to produce a record 16.45 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 (October-September), up sharply from 14.6 in 1994/95, according to domestic industry estimates.
India consumes about 13 million tonnes of sugar every year.
The sugar industry has signed contracts for the export of one million tonnes of sugar out of 1995/96 production. The government has authorised exports of a similar quantity in 1996/97.
Jain said the supply of sugar at cheap rates could be restricted to the poorest of the poor.
Under the present system the industry is forced to supply sugar to the poor at prices which are set by the government and far below the cost of production, Jain said.
